doc.title: Paquito D'Rivera — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Preparing himself: lifelong symphony experience and feeling the beat
summary: Having worked with symphonies since childhood, he understands their weight, and contrasts that with a Black Cuban sense of rhythm.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: It’s obvious that process for you, to where you’ve had to almost train yourself to recognize these kinds of things—
In order to make these things work. How have you gone about doing that?
How have you gone about training yourself, gearing yourself to that way of thinking, of making those compromises?

It is in my spirit; I have been working with symphony orchestras since I was a kid, so I know how I work. I know how heavy the symphony orchestra is; it’s a very heavy thing, and I remember somebody saying that harmony and the Cleveland Orchestra, you see that when he do that, that when they see the harmony doing this, and the orchestra, and they say oooo[ imitates sound]. For me that doesn’t make any sense. You know, I am used to bahhh [imitates sound], you know, but that is the Count Basie Orchestra, that is something else. So I am a understanding that the way it work, you do like ooooo [imitates sound]. I hate it; I don’t like it because I am a Black guy born in Cuba. So for me the rhythm is [imitates rhythm]. You know, one is one, oooo
